title: Emaki 絵巻
section: From the IDE to the ADE
text:
From the IDE to the ADE



               Activity Bar       File Browser      Outline     Timeline            Code             Terminal         Agent Chat            




IDE integrated development environment

An IDE is built for writing code by hand: many panels, a steep learning curve, and real effort to set up. With agents, you write less code and run fewer commands yourself, yet the editor still takes the middle of the screen and most of your attention. The agent chat and git sit at the edges, and there is no way to manage the agent’s sessions at all.







       Emaki                             New Chat     Projects                    Chats       Agent Chat                                Files             Outline            Shell Terminal            Agent Terminal   




ADE agentic development environment

Emaki, an agentic development environment, turns this around. The agent chat is the main panel, rendered with care, and four panels open beside it when you need them: files, outline, shell terminal and agent terminal. Sessions are listed under their projects, where you can manage them and keep them safe from automatic deletion.

title: Settings
text:
Appearance and Fonts
Appearance follows the system or pins light or dark, and the accent is one of seven: periwinkle, orchid, rose, amber, moss, jade or teal. Fonts has eight faces for the chat and four monospace faces for code and the terminal, all under the Open Font License, and one text size for all three.

title: Settings
text:
New sessions
Each agent’s mode, model and effort to begin with. The pills under the composer change them for one session.

title: Settings
text:
Composer, Terminal, Files
Each one’s own switches: which key sends and which languages are spell-checked; the terminal’s scheme, its cursor, and whether a selection copies itself; format on save and its formatters.

title: Settings
text:
Updates and About
Updates checks daily, or now, and installs the new version itself. About says which version this is and who makes it.

An entry and the outline button answer the pointer.

title: Outline Panel
text:
Entries
One entry per prompt, under a heading for each day: the time on a small plate, then three to five words for what you asked. A short prompt is shown as it is. A long one is labeled by the agent’s small model, Haiku for Claude Code and Codex’s light model for Codex, in a session of its own, so nothing enters yours. Labels are asked for the entries in view, a few at a time, and kept for good, so each prompt is asked about once.

title: Outline Panel
text:
Going back
Click an entry and the chat glides to that round. As you scroll, the entry in view wears the accent, so the outline always says where you are. The panel shares the left side with the files: one shows at a time, and one takes the other’s place without moving the chat.

title: Get Started
text:
Open a project
Pick a folder, choose the agent, and type. That is a session, in that folder, and its tab and its row in the sidebar appear at once. Or pick up one the agent already has: every session on the machine is listed under its project, from both agents. The first launch copies every Claude Code transcript into ~/.emaki/archive, and each later launch catches up, so a session the agent has deleted is still here. See Projects.

Files and outline share the left side, one at a time; the two terminals share the right.

title: Get Started
text:
What it keeps
Everything is under ~/.emaki:







archive/
every Claude Code session, copied byte for byte


logs/
each session rendered as markdown


search.db
the full-text index


config.json
your settings



Only archive/ cannot be rebuilt. That is the folder to back up.
Emaki sets one thing in Claude Code’s settings: its status line, which feeds the status bar under the composer. emaki-core statusline restore puts yours back.

title: Chats
text:

The tool call, the plus, the mode and the effort answer the pointer.

title: Chats
text:
The transcript
Prompts, replies, tool calls, thoughts and subagents, laid out like the Claude app. Your prompts sit in a bubble with a tail, replies run the width, and code blocks are colored with a copy button. A tool call is a card, its badge colored by what it does, and three or more in a row fold into one line with a tally. Explain puts one plain sentence on an opaque call, asked of the agent’s small model in a session of its own, so nothing of it enters yours.
While the agent works, approvals, questions and plans arrive as cards at the end, and anything the window has no card for shows on its terminal card. ⌘F finds in the chat; ⌘G steps to the next hit.

title: Chats
text:
The composer
Type and send: ↩︎ or ⌘↩︎, your choice, and ⇧↩︎ is a new line. A session running in a terminal gets the message through the agent’s inbox; a finished one resumes under Emaki. Drafts survive quitting.

Attach by paste, drop or the + button. A picture shows as a thumbnail, any other file as a chip with its name and size.
@ picks a file or folder from the project, as the agent’s own prompt does.
/ lists the slash commands and skills the agent knows. A command that acts alone runs on ↩︎; a skill goes into the message.
Spelling and grammar are checked as you type, with corrections on the right-click menu.


To talk instead of typing, in Emaki or any other app, there is Kotoba, our dictation app for the Mac.

title: Chats
text:
Mode, model and effort
Three pills under the composer, in the agent’s own colors, each opening its list in place. ⇧Tab steps the mode, as it does in the terminal. A new session starts with the defaults set in Settings, New sessions; the pills change them for this one.

title: Chats
text:
The status bar
The row under the composer says how much of the context window is used and where the five-hour and seven-day limits stand, colored at the thresholds the agent’s own status line uses, for Claude Code and Codex alike. Notices land there too: what a command did, or why something could not be done.

title: About
text:
An emaki (絵巻) is a Japanese picture handscroll: a long painted scene held between two rolls, read by winding it from one to the other, a span at a time. It is a good name for a window whose job is an agent chat too long to see at once.
The app’s icon is a handscroll seen from the front, with an agent chat on its sheet: the agent on the left with its spark, your reply on the right. This one carries a landscape instead, and winds as you move across it.

title: About
text:
Why it exists
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays, thirty by default, with no warning. Every other tool in this space reads ~/.claude/projects and stops there, so they all inherit that expiry.
So Emaki copies first and renders second. The archive sweep runs before anything else touches a session, for exactly this reason: if rendering fails, the bytes are already safe. The archive is not a backup but a peer source: live and kept transcripts are read together, so a session Claude Code has deleted stays listed, searchable and readable, marked kept.
Compaction, for what it is worth, was never the threat: it appends a boundary and keeps writing to the same file, leaving the earlier rows intact.

title: About
text:
How it is built
Rust, with GPUI, the Zed editor’s UI framework, and gpui-component for the window. There is no daemon, no browser and no hook.
crates/emaki-core   everything without a window, and the CLI
crates/emaki-app    the window
vendor/             gpui-component, with a few changes of ours
scripts/            packaging, the icon, the status line
The core works in this order:

Adapters, one per agent, find each agent’s sessions on disk.
Archive copies Claude Code’s byte for byte, before anything else touches them.
Build parses the JSONL transcript into a model of rounds, items and tool calls. The transcript is the only source of truth.
Render writes that model as markdown under ~/.emaki/logs.
Search indexes every item in SQLite FTS5.

The app reads the same model and draws it. A file watcher says when to look again. To reply, it writes to a terminal session’s inbox, or runs a headless agent of its own that appends to the same transcript.

title: About
text:
Where it is going
Three stages. The first is a complete app for Claude Code: permanent history, organization by recency, project and agent, readable chats, and an explanation on any step. The second is the public release and the feedback that comes with it. The third extends the same to Codex, Kimi and the other mainstream coding agents, so Emaki works across all of them.
Codex arrived in v0.2.0, ahead of its stage; the releases are the honest record of where things stand.

title: About
text:
Who makes it



Alkaline Software
Two data scientists making basic software. Alkaline is the other word for basic, as a high pH is, and basic is what the software means to be: the things that should plainly exist. Emaki is one of them, a development environment for the agentic era that anyone who works with agents can use.



Dr John Paul Helveston
Associate Professor of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering at George Washington University.



Dr Pingfan Hu
Data scientist and developer at George Washington University, advised by John Paul.

title: About
text:
Credits
The home page’s figure follows the line-drawing manner of hairline’s figures: nothing filled, no words, what is far is dimmer, and one bright mark.
Icons are Tabler’s outline set, drawn at a stroke of 1.75 where Tabler’s own is 2, in the app and on this site. The file tree’s icons are Catppuccin’s. The code colors are Rosé Pine’s hues, retinted for contrast. The terminal keeps Kaku’s cream in the light appearance. Every face the app carries is under the SIL Open Font License, and so are this site’s: Source Serif 4, JetBrains Mono and Belleza. The site is made with Quarto.

title: Agent Terminal Panel
text:
The agent’s own screen
Every session Emaki runs has a terminal behind it: Claude Code’s hidden one, or Codex’s joined to its driver. This panel draws it whole, at the chat’s right, so you can watch the agent work as you would in the CLI, and type into it when you want to. It is the same terminal the window reads and types into, so nothing is doubled.
Open it with nothing running and it starts the agent (Claude Code); where one cannot start, a turn running in a terminal of your own, or an archived session, it says why. Whatever the agent asks that the window has no card for can be answered here. It shares the right side with the shell terminal: one shows at a time.

title: Files Panel
text:
Emaki     New Session All Sessions Agents Projects emaki31          4 2 Temporary10         Fable 5.1  Explain           Context                Files main 2      M M  U       main.rs       New branch     ChangesHistory mainPush1  M U M  *  Commit 2 files notes.md     


A file, the branch, the Changes count and the files button answer the pointer.

title: Files Panel
text:
The tree
The project’s folder, with git’s marks on it: a letter on a changed file, a dot on a folder with changes under it, ignored files dimmed. It works like a file manager: drag in from Finder, drag rows to move them, cut, copy, duplicate, remove (⌘⌫, to the Trash) and undo (⌘Z). New File and New Folder are at the head, and a file the agent writes appears as it lands.

title: Files Panel
text:
Open and edit
Click a file and it opens in a pane between the tree and the chat; click it again to put it away. The enlarge button gives the pane the chat’s room. ⌘S saves, ⌘W closes, and nothing unsaved is lost without asking. Format on save covers ten languages and is off until you turn it on.
Code comes with line numbers, colors and a gutter mark per git change, with a card to see or revert it. Every kind of file is drawn for what it is:


Code every language, colored
Markdown as it reads, or as written
CSV and TSV a grid you can edit in place
Parquet a table with each column’s type
Word pages you can type in and format
Excel cells with their number formats
PowerPoint slides as they look
PDF sharp at any width, with search and page previews
HTML in the system’s web view
Pictures at their own size

title: Files Panel
text:
Git
In a repository the branch is named at the tree’s head. Click it to switch, make a branch (⌘⇧N) or publish one; Fetch and Pull sit at the list’s foot. A switch with uncommitted changes asks whether to leave them or bring them along, and goes through only when every change lands where you asked.
The Changes pill (⌘⇧G) opens the sheet: tick the files, write the message, commit (⌘↩︎), push (⌘P). History browses the commits: Undo takes back the newest while the remote does not have it, Revert takes back any one as a new commit. Nothing is committed, pushed or pulled without a click that says so.

title: Projects
text:
Emaki     New Session All Sessions Agents Projects emaki31           4 2 Temporary10          Fable 5.1  Explain            Context 5h · 49% 7d · 56%                       


The folder, a session and New Session answer the pointer.

title: Projects
text:
Projects
A project is a folder you have run an agent in. The sidebar lists them all, the newest first, pinned ones on top. Click a project to unfold its sessions. The plus on its row starts a new session there (⌘T in the project you are in, ⌘N anywhere). A project with a live session wears the accent and opens by itself.
Right-click a project to archive or delete its sessions, open it in Finder, or hide it. Hidden projects and the system’s temporary folders sit under their own headings at the foot. Nothing in a project’s own folder is ever touched.

title: Projects
text:
Sessions
Each session is a row under its project: the agent’s mark, lit while it runs, a dot for where it stands, the title, and a bar at the left when it has a tab. Claude Code and Codex sessions sit side by side, each read from its own files.
All Sessions (⌘L) lists every project and every session with the day it was last touched, archived ones under their own heading, and narrows to one agent. Select many at once (⌘-click, ⇧-click, or drag a rectangle), then archive or delete them together.

title: Projects
text:
Kept and archived
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after thirty days. Emaki copies every one into ~/.emaki/archive the first time it sees it, so a session the agent has deleted is still listed, searchable and readable, marked kept. Codex deletes nothing by age, so its sessions are read in place.
Archive a session and the agent leaves it alone until you unarchive it. Delete moves every copy to the Trash. Renaming a session renames it for the agent too.

title: Projects
text:
Search
⌘K searches every session on the machine. One hit per prompt, paragraph, thought or tool call, so a hit lands on the thing you remembered, in live and kept sessions alike.

title: Projects
text:
Tabs
Every open session is a tab, grouped by project. ⌘1 to ⌘9 switch, ⌘W closes, ⌘⇧T brings back the last one closed, and a drag reorders them.

title: Shell Terminal Panel
section: A shell where the work is
text:
A shell where the work is
Your login shell, opened in the session’s folder, at the chat’s right. Shells are tabs: the + or ⌘T opens one, ⌘W closes it, ⌘K clears the screen, and a drag reorders them. They stay open until you close them or quit.
Paste a picture and it lands as the path of a file. A selection can copy itself when you let go (Settings, Terminal). Mouse-aware programs take clicks and scrolls, and the Mac’s line keys work (⌘←, ⌘→, ⌘⌫). The look is Kaku’s, in the window’s own colors and face.
The same shell opens beside the install steps on the Agents page, for the commands they give. It shares the right side with the agent terminal: one shows at a time.
